t.2.57.1: Then King Daśaratha, his mind stricken with grief, regaining consciousness after a moment, fell into deep thought.
t.2.57.2: And because of the exile of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, affliction entered him who was like Vāsava, as darkness enters the mighty sun.
t.2.57.3: On the sixth night after Rāma had gone forth into the forest, King Daśaratha, at midnight, recalling the evil deed he had once done, spoke these words to Kausalyā, who was stricken with grief for her son.
t.2.57.4: Whatever one does, O auspicious lady, whether good or evil, O gentle one, that very fruit born of his own deeds the doer receives.
t.2.57.5: He who, at the commencement of his deeds, does not know the weightiness or lightness of matters, nor the fruit or the fault of his actions, is called a child.
t.2.57.6: Someone cuts down a grove of mango trees and waters the palāśa trees instead; having seen their blossoms, he grows greedy for fruit, and he grieves when the fruit appears.
t.2.57.7: I, that very fool, having cut down a mango grove, watered the palāśa trees; having abandoned Rāma just when the fruit was coming, I grieve afterwards, wicked-minded as I am.
t.2.57.8: O Kausalyā, it was I, a young prince armed with a bow, renowned as 'the prince who shoots by sound,' who committed this sin. Now, O queen, this sorrow of my own making has come upon me.
t.2.57.9: Just as poison might be eaten here by a child out of delusion, so too the fruit that comes of shooting at a mere sound was unknown to me.
t.2.57.10: O queen, you were not yet married, and I was the crown prince. Then the rainy season arrived, which heightens passion and desire.
t.2.57.11: For the sun, having drawn up the moisture of the earth and scorched the world with its rays, now enters the dreadful quarter frequented by the departed dead.
t.2.57.12: The heat vanished at once, and glossy clouds came into view; then all the frogs, deer and peacocks rejoiced.
t.2.57.14: In that most pleasant season, bearing my bow and arrows and riding in my chariot, I went along the river Sarayū, having set my mind on exercise.
t.2.57.13: Covered again and again by the water that had fallen and was still falling, the mountain, alive with excited peacocks, shone like an ocean.
t.2.57.16: Then, in the darkness, beyond the range of my sight, I heard in the water the sound of a pitcher being filled, like the sound of an elephant trumpeting.
t.2.57.15: With my senses unsubdued, I was eager to kill, at night by the watering place, a buffalo, or an elephant come down to the river, or some other wild beast.
t.2.57.17: Then I drew out a blazing arrow like a venomous serpent, and I loosed that sharpened shaft, which was like a venomous serpent.
t.2.57.19: I came at night to this secluded river to fetch water. By whom have I been struck with an arrow? To whom, indeed, have I done any wrong?
t.2.57.18: There at dawn a clear voice of a forest-dweller arose; a human voice was heard there of one falling into the water, crying "Alas, alas! How could a weapon fall upon an ascetic such as me?"
t.2.57.20: For how can slaying with a weapon be ordained for one such as me, a sage who has laid down the rod and lives in the forest on forest fare?
t.2.57.21: Who could have any purpose in slaying me, who bear only a heavy mass of matted hair and wear garments of bark and deerskin? Or what wrong have I ever done to him?
t.2.57.22: No one would regard as good a deed undertaken in this way, fruitless and bound up with nothing but harm, just as no one would think well of a man who violates his guru's bed.
t.2.57.24: This aged couple, long supported by me: when I have met my death, what means of living will they find?
t.2.57.23: I do not grieve so much for this ending of my own life; it is for both my mother and my father that I grieve, now that one such as I has met this fate.
t.2.57.25: My aged mother and father, and I too, struck down by a single arrow: by what utterly foolish man of undisciplined mind have we all been slain?
t.2.57.27: Having come to that place, dejected in spirit and deeply troubled, I saw on the bank of the Sarayū an ascetic struck down by my arrow.
t.2.57.26: Hearing that piteous voice, I, who had always longed for righteousness, was stricken with anguish, and the bow with its arrow fell from my hands to the ground.
t.2.57.28: Looking up at me with his eyes as I stood terrified and troubled in mind, he spoke these cruel words, as if wishing to burn me with his fiery power.
t.2.57.29: O king, what wrong have I, dwelling in the forest, done to you, that you have struck me down as I was seeking to fetch water for the sake of my elders?
t.2.57.30: Indeed, by a single arrow striking me in a vital spot, two are slain, both blind and aged: my mother and my father.
t.2.57.31: Surely those two, feeble and blind, thirsting and waiting for me, will long endure a painful thirst born of hope.
t.2.57.32: Surely there is no fruit to be gained from austerity or from sacred learning, since my father does not know that I lie fallen upon the ground.
t.2.57.33: Even though he knows, what could he do, powerless and unable to move, just as one mountain is powerless to save another mountain that is being split apart?
t.2.57.34: Go quickly yourself, Rāghava, and tell my father, so that in his anger he may not burn you up, as a blazing fire burns a forest.
t.2.57.35: This narrow footpath, O king, leads to where my father's hermitage lies. Go there and appease him, so that he, enraged, may not curse you.
t.2.57.36: Draw out the arrow from me, O king; the sharpened shaft presses upon my vital part as a rush of water presses upon a soft, high riverbank.
t.2.57.37: I am not a twice-born, O king; let there be no anguish in your mind. I was born of a vaiśya father upon a śūdra mother, O lord of the land.
t.2.57.38: As he spoke thus with great difficulty, his vitals pierced by the arrow, and as he lay writhing and bent in agony, I drew that arrow out.
t.2.57.39: Then, gracious lady, having lamented in anguish, I beheld him lying in the Sarayū, his limbs drenched with water, wounded in his vitals and gasping without pause, and I was overwhelmed with despair.
